description_full: NVIDIA Corporation operates as a data center scale AI infrastructure company in the United States, Taiwan, China, Hong Kong, Europe, and internationally. It operates through Compute & Networking, and Graphics segments. The Compute & Networking segment provides data center accelerated computing and networking platforms and artificial intelligence solutions and software, and automotive platforms and autonomous and electric vehicle solutions, including software. The Graphics segment offers GeForce GPUs for gaming and PCs; Quadro/NVIDIA RTX GPUs for enterprise workstation graphics. The company's products are used in gaming, professional visualization, data center, and automotive markets. It sells its products to original equipment manufacturers, original device manufacturers, system integrators and distributors, independent software vendors, cloud service providers, add-in board manufacturers, distributors, automotive manufacturers and tier-1 automotive suppliers, and other ecosystem participants. It has a collaboration with Cisco to develop Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP), a high-density optical module pluggable transceiver. It has a collaboration with ChipAgents to develop Build-A-Chip-Bench, a benchmark for AI agents carrying chip design tasks and The Company has a strategic alliance with MediaTek to build the next generations of AI computing platforms. NVIDIA Corporation was incorporated in 1993 and is headquartered in Santa Clara, California.

financial_summary: NVIDIA Corporation is a mega-cap technology business with a $3.9T market cap on $215.9B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +100% over the past three years and +46% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +3.5pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 111% against a 13% cost of capital — a 98-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 59% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $96.7B in free cash flow — roughly 45 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.86× cash conversion.
Accruals are elevated at +8.4% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 4.0% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.3% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 111% clears the cost of capital of 12.7% by 98pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.63).
It runs a 59% gross margin and converts 45% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (+8.4% of assets).
ROE of 76% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.3x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 23pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 8.6% of revenue on R&D and 3.0% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $2.1B (0% of market cap).
Warning signs: a Beneish M-score that flags possible earnings manipulation.

growth: Revenue has compounded at 66.9% over 5 years and 45.7% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 40%).
At current returns, reinvesting 31% of profits supports about 30.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 1% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 42%.
Capex runs 2.1x depreciation (2.8% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 109, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.0%, and institutions hold 71%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (22 sales, net $960.0M sold).
